title: Cybersecurity Design and Data Protection

sources.title: NIST SP 800-204, Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems
sources.scope: Read pp. 1, 6-8, 15-16, 17-19, 21-24, 25-30, 33-36. Microservice API security features, identity/access management, discovery, secure communications, monitoring, gateway/service mesh, disadvantages, threats and strategies.

sources.title: AWS Security and Compliance: Shared Responsibility
sources.scope: Read shared responsibility passages: AWS security of the cloud and customer security in the cloud; AWS manages facilities/hardware while customer retains control of content, platforms, applications, systems, and networks.

sources.title: Docker Docs: What is a container?
sources.scope: Read explanation and Containers versus VMs: containers are isolated processes sharing a kernel; a VM includes an operating system and its own kernel; VMs and containers may be used together.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Hash Functions
sources.scope: Read hash definition mapping arbitrary-length messages to fixed-length digests, approved FIPS hash families, stated expected hash properties, and collision-resistance strength table.

sources.title: NIST: Blockchain
sources.scope: Read NIST description of shared tamper-evident/tamper-resistant ledgers, blocks cryptographically linked to prior blocks, replicated nodes, validation and consensus; NIST notes different implementations and research into security guarantees.

sources.title: RFC 9162: Certificate Transparency Version 2.0
sources.scope: Read Merkle-tree passages: efficient inclusion and consistency proofs, append-only log property, and detecting log misbehavior. This is a concrete hash-tree integrity mechanism, not evidence that ledger inputs are true.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, Key Management
sources.scope: Read publication description on key types, security services, cryptographic keying material protection and key-management practices. Landing metadata is used only for those stated scopes.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-4, Digital Identity Guidelines
sources.scope: Read publication description identifying identity proofing, authentication, enrollment, authenticators, management, authentication protocols, federation, and assertions; use only for these scope distinctions.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture
sources.scope: Read NIST summary: no implicit trust based solely on network location or asset ownership; supports explicit per-resource access framing and segmentation discussion.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide
sources.scope: Read publication overview describing contingency planning process, plan development, organizational resiliency, and relationship to incident/emergency plans; not used as evidence for backup copy mechanics.

sources.title: NISTIR 8259A IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline
sources.scope: Read NIST abstract: baseline device capabilities support common controls protecting devices, device data, systems, and ecosystems; detailed capability descriptions not retrieved.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: Mandatory Access Control
sources.scope: Read glossary definition: uniform policy across subjects/objects constrains information passing, privilege delegation, security-attribute changes, and access-rule changes, with trusted-subject exceptions.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: Discretionary Access Control
sources.scope: Read glossary definition: object owner or authorized controller decides which subjects receive which object access rights.

sources.title: NIST CSRC Glossary: Role-Based Access Control
sources.scope: Read glossary definition: user access follows role-linked authorizations typically reflecting organizational functions; role hierarchies may inherit permissions.

sources.title: RFC 20: ASCII format for Network Interchange
sources.scope: Read for ASCII character encoding context only; not evidence for substitution-cipher security.

sources.title: Harvard CS50x: Caesar
sources.scope: Read Problem to Solve and the rotation formula (p+k) modulo 26, wraparound and reverse-shift examples, plus the explicit warning that this is not secure by modern standards. The ATTACK example is original arithmetic independently checked from that rule.

pages.title: Cloud responsibility and service models
notes: Cloud moves workloads; it does not remove customer duties.
Provider secures cloud facilities, hardware, managed layers.
Customer secures data, identities, settings, and lawful use.
Exact responsibility depends on service and configuration.
IaaS rents compute, storage, and network infrastructure.
IaaS customer normally manages guest OS and applications.
PaaS provider manages platform/runtime; customer manages app.
SaaS vendor runs app; customer manages users and data.
More abstraction reduces customer control and admin work.

pages.title: Cloud choices, effects, and shared duties
notes: Example: IaaS customer patches guest; provider patches host.
SaaS customer controls account access and sharing settings.
Provider controls do not correct customer misconfiguration.
Public cloud can scale quickly without owning facilities.
Costs shift toward usage; careless usage can raise bills.
Cloud dependence adds provider, network, and outage risks.
Classify data before selecting cloud storage or region.
Review contract, duties, audit, and recovery options.
AWS calls this security of the cloud versus in the cloud.
A cloud service is not automatically safer than local hosting.

pages.title: Microservices and API security
notes: Microservices are small components communicating over APIs.
An API endpoint accepts requests for a defined operation.
Each reachable endpoint adds code and attack surface.
Authenticate the caller; separately authorize each action.
A valid login does not grant every endpoint permission.
Service-to-service calls also need identity and access rules.
NIST lists authentication and access management as core needs.
Secure channels help protect service communications.
Mutually authenticate services; authorize each API operation.

pages.title: Distributed policy and complexity
notes: Many services multiply routes, keys, versions, and policies.
Service discovery locates changing service instances.
Incorrect discovery can direct requests to hostile endpoints.
Gateways centralize some edge checks and traffic controls.
Internal services still require correct authorization checks.
A service mesh can package communication/security functions.
Frameworks reduce repetition but add configuration complexity.
Monitoring and rate limits help detect or constrain abuse.
Microservices scale independently, not securely by default.
Review boundaries; test denied and allowed API calls.

practice.prompt: A SaaS team assumes the vendor controls user sharing. What is wrong?
practice.answer: The provider runs the application, but the customer still manages accounts, data, and many sharing settings. Review the service-specific responsibility split and restrict access.

practice.prompt: Why is API login insufficient to protect every microservice endpoint?
practice.answer: Authentication establishes a caller identity; authorization decides whether that identity may perform this operation. Each endpoint needs an appropriate policy, including service-to-service calls.

pages.title: Segmentation and trust boundaries
notes: Physical segmentation separates equipment, cabling, or sites.
Logical segmentation partitions shared gear with rules.
VLANs separate layer-two broadcast domains on shared switches.
ACLs and firewalls govern traffic across segment boundaries.
Segmentation can limit lateral movement after compromise.
A VLAN alone is not encryption or identity authentication.
Rules must allow required paths and block unauthorized paths.
NIST zero trust rejects trust based only on network location.
Segmentation complements, not replaces, access checks.

pages.title: Test segment policy and verify boundaries
notes: Identify assets, owners, data flows, boundaries first.
Permit only needed source, destination, protocol, service.
Test intended communication after policy changes.
Test forbidden communication from each relevant segment.
Monitor boundary traffic for unexpected communication.
Physical separation may share unsafe administration.
Logical separation may fail through bad rules or trunking.
Document exceptions, owners, and review dates.
Choose controls from threat and cost needs.
A subnet or VLAN is not a complete security boundary.

pages.title: Virtual machines and containers
notes: A hypervisor allocates host resources to virtual machines.
A VM typically runs a guest OS with its own kernel.
Containers isolate processes and package dependencies.
Containers commonly share the host operating-system kernel.
VMs add guest OS overhead; containers can be lighter.
VM isolation can fail through hypervisor flaws or settings.
A container kernel escape may threaten other host containers.
Patch hosts, hypervisors, guest systems, images, libraries.
Limit privileges, mounts, capabilities, and network access.

pages.title: IoT risks and safer deployment
notes: VMs and containers may be combined on one host.
Isolation reduces some risks; it is not an absolute guarantee.
IoT means networked sensors, cameras, appliances, and devices.
Default passwords and open services expose IoT devices.
Old firmware and weak updates leave known flaws unpatched.
Constrained power or memory can limit security monitoring.
Excess device data collection creates privacy risk.
Inventory device, owner, firmware, network, support end date.
Change defaults; disable unused features; patch and isolate.
NIST baseline groups device capabilities supporting controls.

practice.prompt: Two container apps share a host. What isolation limit matters?
practice.answer: They commonly share the host kernel, unlike VMs with guest kernels. A kernel escape can cross container boundaries; patch the host and limit privileges, while choosing stronger isolation when justified.

practice.prompt: Name two IoT risks and a practical response to each.
practice.answer: Default credentials call for changing passwords and disabling unused access; unsupported firmware calls for isolation, monitoring, and planned replacement. Network isolation reduces exposure but does not fix device flaws.

pages.title: Backup methods and recovery
notes: A backup is a separate recoverable copy of selected data.
Full copies selected data; restore is straightforward.
Incremental copies changes since the most recent backup.
Restore a full backup, then each incremental in sequence.
Differential copies changes since the last full backup.
Restore a full backup and the latest differential copy.
Differentials grow until another full backup is made.
Test restores; unreadable copies do not protect.
Keep isolated or offline copies to resist ransomware.

pages.title: RAID, UPS, and CIA design cases
notes: RAID combines disks for performance or fault tolerance.
RAID 1 mirrors; RAID 5 tolerates one disk failure.
RAID 6 tolerates two disk failures; RAID 0 has no redundancy.
RAID cannot protect from deletion, malware, theft, or fire.
RAID is not backup; keep independent, versioned copies.
UPS battery bridges brief outages and enables safe shutdown.
Confidentiality: encrypt backups and restrict key access.
Integrity: detect changes with trusted hashes or signatures.
Availability: UPS and restores limit outage impact.
No single safeguard guarantees all three CIA goals.

pages.title: Security testing and architecture
notes: Testing checks controls against stated needs and threats.
Design review traces assets, identities, flows, boundaries.
Configuration review finds excess access and weak settings.
Scanners find known issues; validate findings and rank risk.
Static analysis examines code without executing it.
Dynamic tests exercise a running application or service.
Pen tests simulate scoped attacks with authorization.
Methods have blind spots; combine them according to risk.
Test staging systems with written scope and stop conditions.

pages.title: Evidence, remediation, and retesting
notes: Record affected asset, evidence, impact, owner, priority.
Fix underlying cause rather than only hiding an alert.
Retest the original path and nearby paths after a fix.
Track exceptions, residual risk, deadlines, and approvals.
Recovery plans assign roles, priorities, and restore order.
Set recovery time and acceptable data-loss targets.
Exercise recovery without risking live data or systems.
Use fictional scenario; check backup chain completeness.
Expected: team identifies restore order, keys, dependencies.
A passed scan or tabletop is not proof of total security.

practice.prompt: Which is safer to restore: full plus incremental, or RAID alone?
practice.answer: A full plus complete incremental chain provides versioned recovery; RAID mainly handles some disk failures and mirrors unwanted deletion or corruption. Keep independent backups and test restores.

practice.prompt: A scan finds no vulnerabilities. Is the architecture secure?
practice.answer: No. Scans have coverage and detection limits. Combine design, configuration, code, and authorized runtime testing; validate findings and retest fixes.

pages.title: Symmetric and public-key cryptography
notes: Cryptography uses algorithms and keys to protect information.
Encryption transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext.
Decryption with the right key recovers the plaintext.
Symmetric cryptography uses one shared secret key both ways.
It is efficient; parties must protect and share the secret.
Public-key cryptography uses a related key pair.
Public key may be shared; private key must remain protected.
Encrypt to recipient's public key; private key decrypts.
This provides confidentiality, not sender proof alone.

pages.title: Signatures, exchange, and key limits
notes: Signer uses private key; others verify with public key.
Signatures can support integrity and key-possession checks.
A signature does not make the signed statement true.
Key exchange establishes a shared secret over a channel.
Unauthenticated exchange risks an active intermediary attack.
Certificates can bind a public key to a named identity.
Validate certificate chain, name, dates, and intended use.
Protect, rotate, revoke, and recover keys by policy.
Hybrid TLS pairs key agreement with symmetric data encryption.
Key loss blocks decryption; compromise threatens protection.

pages.title: Caesar and substitution ciphers
notes: A shift cipher moves each alphabet letter by a fixed amount.
Caesar is a shift cipher, often shown with shift three.
Using +3: A becomes D, B becomes E, and X becomes A.
Wrap after Z: Y becomes B and Z becomes C.
ATTACK with +3 becomes DWWDFN; reverse shift recovers it.
Substitution replaces letters using a fixed alphabet mapping.
Caesar is one simple special case of substitution.
Repeated patterns and frequencies reveal toy ciphers.
Small keyspaces are searchable; these ciphers are not secure.

pages.title: Hashing, blockchain, and trust limits
notes: Hash maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest.
Hashing is not encryption; there is no decryption key.
Collision: two distinct inputs have the same digest.
Collision resistance makes finding one hard in practice.
It is not a promise that collisions are impossible.
A trusted digest can help detect changed data.
A hash alone does not prove who created the data.
Blockchain links blocks by hash and consensus rules.
NIST: shared ledgers are tamper-evident, not truth-proof.
RFC 9162 Merkle proofs check log inclusion and consistency.

practice.prompt: Encrypt a message to Pat and sign it: which keys are used?
practice.answer: Encrypt using Pat's public key so Pat can decrypt with Pat's private key. Sign with the sender's private key; verify using the sender's public key. Protect keys and authenticate their identity binding.

practice.prompt: Decode DWWDFN under Caesar shift +3 and assess security.
practice.answer: Shift each letter back three: ATTACK. This demonstrates reversible substitution only; frequency patterns and a tiny keyspace make it unsuitable for modern security.

pages.title: Three states of data
notes: Data at rest is stored on disk, device, backup, or database.
Protect stored data with encryption and account permissions.
Data in transit moves between devices or services.
Use protected channels and verify communicating endpoints.
Data in use is actively processed by an application.
Limit process, memory, screen, and log exposure.
Encryption at rest may not protect data after unlock.
Transit encryption does not protect a compromised endpoint.
Select controls based on sensitivity and threat model.

pages.title: MAC, DAC, and RBAC models
notes: MAC means mandatory access control under central policy.
Labels and clearance can govern classified document access.
Ordinary users cannot freely override mandatory policy.
DAC means discretionary access control assigned by owner.
Example: file owner shares a document with colleagues.
Sharing can propagate access; review inherited permissions.
RBAC means role-based access control tied to job duties.
Payroll role reads pay data; approver role authorizes pay.
Assign needed roles; remove stale role membership.
Models can coexist; choose for risk and workflow.

pages.title: Authentication and MFA
notes: Authentication checks control of an identity's authenticator.
Authorization decides which resource action is permitted.
Accounting records access and actions for review.
MFA combines distinct types: know, have, or are.
Two passwords are both knowledge, not two factors.
A password plus authenticator token is two different factors.
MFA reduces password-only risk but does not stop every attack.
Phishing-resistant authenticators reduce credential relay.
Protect enrollment, recovery, and authenticator revocation.

pages.title: Certificates, tokens, and policy
notes: Certificate binds a public key to an identity under CA trust.
Validate chain, service name, dates, and certificate purpose.
Certificate authentication does not authorize every action.
Token carries an assertion or credential to a resource.
Check token issuer, signature, audience, expiry, and scope.
Bearer token may be used by whoever steals it; protect it.
Short expiry limits exposure but does not prevent theft.
Authorize each API action using identity and least privilege.
Revoke compromised credentials and review resulting access.
NIST 800-63-4 covers proofing, authenticators, and federation.

practice.prompt: A file owner shares a folder directly. Which model is illustrated?
practice.answer: DAC: an owner grants access at discretion. Review inheritance and remove unnecessary access. MAC instead applies central labels/rules; RBAC assigns rights through roles.

practice.prompt: A valid certificate authenticates a user. Does it grant database write access?
practice.answer: No. Certificate validation can authenticate a key under CA trust; authorization separately checks whether that identity may write. A scoped token or policy must grant that action.

lab.title: Local design and data-protection tabletop
steps: Use fictional cloud app with three API services and sample records.
Mark provider/customer duties for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS versions.
Draw physical/logical segments and label allowed service paths.
Compare one VM boundary with containers sharing its kernel.
Choose full plus incremental or differential backup and restore order.
Assign fictional roles; test allowed and denied record actions.
Calculate Caesar +3 for CAT, then reverse it; discuss weakness.
Hash two harmless sample strings locally; compare digests.
Identify which claims need identity, trusted key, or external evidence.
expected: Customer duties remain for cloud identity, data, and settings.
Every endpoint has authentication and least-privilege authorization.
Segment rules permit required flows and block others.
VM guest kernel differs from containers' shared host kernel.
Backup restore chain is explicit; RAID is not substituted for backup.
Role policy denies unauthorized edits and limits auditor access.
CAT shifts to FDW; reverse shift returns CAT; toy is not secure.
Hash change can indicate changed bytes but proves neither source nor truth.

limitations: CS-SD-01 cloud responsibility varies by provider, service model, contract, and configuration; AWS is an illustrative provider source.
NIST SP 800-34 publication overview was read, but not its detailed backup-method sections; full/incremental/differential mechanics are basic explanatory notes, not attributed to that overview.
NIST SP 800-57 and SP 800-63 fetched pages expose publication scope/metadata; they do not establish every algorithm or authenticator detail stated here.

The requested NIST hash and blockchain passages were fetched and read. Blockchain security depends on implementation, governance, consensus, keys, and participants; it does not establish truth or guaranteed immutability.
Classical Caesar example is a toy arithmetic illustration, not a modern cryptographic recommendation.
